note.label: Edom: The Robbers of thy people revealed past and present

precepts.why:
The book of Sirach was written by Jesus the son of Sirach, a wise man, around 200 to 175 BC. That is the Greek time period, and the book was written to help fight against Greek influence in the time it was written. So when Sirach speaks of “They that sit upon the mountain of Samaria”, the question is who, during the time of the Greeks, sat upon the mountain of Samaria. Second Maccabees answers it.

“Not long after this the king sent an old man of Athens to compel the Jews to depart from the laws of their fathers, and not to live after the laws of God”. That is the Greek king commanding Judah to depart from the laws of our God and serve the Greek laws and the Greek fashions instead. This is called assimilation, integration, Hellenization: we became Greeks, Greek citizens, like African Americans today. Same thing.

“And to pollute also the temple in Jerusalem, and to call it the temple of Jupiter Olympius”. The Greeks polluted the temple in Jerusalem, in Judah, and called it the temple of Zeus, for Jupiter is Zeus. “And that in Garizim, of Jupiter the Defender of strangers, as they did desire that dwelt in the place.” Garizim is a mount in Samaria. The Greeks built and sat upon Mount Garizim.

So who sat upon the mount in Samaria at this time? The Greeks. Other translations of Sirach 50:26 call them Edomites, verbatim: Edomites that sat upon Samaria. Then Sirach is telling you the Greeks were Edomites.

The rest of the verse follows: “they that dwell among the Philistines” are the Hamites, and “that foolish people that dwell in Sichem” is the northern kingdom, the silly nation that loved the heathen, the not a people of Deuteronomy 32. It is always them trying to take our land. This is war.

precepts.text: Simon the high priest, son of Onias, repaired the house again and fortified the temple. These renowned men earned their names by building back and walking in integrity. Go through Sirach 44 to 50 again on your own; the class only jumped through them.
precepts.point: Of the twelve prophets, let their memorial be blessed, for they comforted Jacob and delivered them by assured hope. Zerubbabel was as a signet on the right hand. Nehemiah, whose renown is great, raised up the fallen walls and re-established the laws so nobody would have the people shopping on the Sabbath. Joseph was a governor of his brethren and a stay of the people.

note.label: Much Is Given, Much Is Required

precepts.why:
After Josias, the twelve prophets, Zorobabel, Neemias and Joseph, Sirach carries the line of renowned men on to the priesthood: “Simon the high priest, the son of Onias, who in his life repaired the house again, and in his days fortified the temple”. Simon repaired the house again. Like Neemias, “who raised up for us the walls that were fallen, and set up the gates and the bars, and raised up our ruins again”, his name is tied to building back what was broken down.

That is how these renowned men earned their names. It was about building back, walking in integrity, moving right. Josias “behaved himself uprightly in the conversion of the people”, not using his position to take advantage of the people or handling the word of God deceitfully. Neemias raised the walls and established the laws again, so nobody would come in trying to get our people to shop on the Sabbath. Simon repaired and fortified the house of God.

So it is with us: “in the time of the ungodly he established the worship of God.” In the midst of all this debauchery we are to establish the worship of God, with no hypocrisy, no covetousness and no murmuring, so that the people see us and say these are those guys we heard about that are going to come back on the earth. That is how you become the famous man.

The class only jumped through these chapters for time’s sake. Go through Sirach 44 to 50 again on your own, because there is a lot more in them.

precepts.text: Two manner of nations my heart abhorreth, and the third is no nation: they that sit upon the mountain of Samaria, the Greeks who ruled it then, they that dwell among the Philistines, and that foolish people that dwell in Sichem. The foolish people of Shechem are the northern kingdom, 'no nation' and 'foolish,' exactly as Moses wrote.
precepts.point: Ephraim allied with Syria against Judah. The head of Syria is Damascus and the head of Damascus is Rezin, and within threescore and five years shall Ephraim be broken, that it be not a people. That is who Moses meant by 'not a people.'

note.label: The Dividing Hatred: the Grafted in Strangers

precepts.why:
Ephraim aligned itself with Syria to attack its own brother Judah, and Isaiah 7:8 is the prophecy against them for it. “For the head of Syria is Damascus”, Syria's capital, “and the head of Damascus is Rezin”, the king of the Syrians at that time, “and within threescore and five years shall Ephraim be broken, that it be not a people.” That is who Moses was talking about when he said the Lord would provoke Israel to jealousy with them which are not a people, with a foolish nation: Ephraim.

Sirach shows the same people by name and place. “There be two manner of nations which my heart abhorreth, and the third is no nation.” Two nations he despises, and the third is no nation at all. “They that sit upon the mountain of Samaria”: in this context that is the Greeks, who ruled over Samaria then, and he says he despises them. “And they that dwell among the Philistines”: the Philistines are Hamites, and he hates them too.

“And that foolish people that dwell in Sichem.” Foolish, and no nation: the very words Moses used, not a people and foolish. Who dwelt in Shechem? The northern kingdom. Shechem is in Samaria, northern kingdom's land, where Abraham built that altar. It is by Sychar, where Christ met the woman at the well, near “the parcel of ground that Jacob gave to his son Joseph”, the land of Ephraim and Manasseh.

So Isaiah says Ephraim would be broken that it be not a people, Hosea calls them Lo-ammi, not my people, and Sirach calls them no nation and foolish. It is the same people every time. And that is why Peter writes to “the strangers scattered” which “in time past were not a people, but are now the people of God”: Christ laid down his life for the other sheep not of Judah's fold, to gather together in one the children of God that were scattered abroad.

note.label: Thankskilling Get Away: A Sign of The World

precepts.why: How do we know the moon in her glory is when she is full? “Simon the high priest, the son of Onias, who in his life repaired the house again”: he was righteous, “and in his days fortified the temple.” In his days, during Simon II’s reign as the high priest, the temple was fortified.

note.label: Thankskilling Get Away: A Sign of The World

precepts.why: “He was as the morning star in the midst of a cloud, and as the moon at the full.” The morning star: that is the sun. And he was as the moon at the full. What does that mean? Read on to verse 11.

note.label: Thankskilling Get Away: A Sign of The World

precepts.why:
“When he put on the robe of honour, and was clothed with the perfection of glory.” That is how we know: the moon at the full is the perfection of glory. When it is full, it is new.

Somebody used that scripture trying to contradict us, but they did not read it properly. It is describing the moon fully full of light, the new moon: full of light, the way it was created. When the moon is perfect, when it is new, it is in its glory. That is how the priest was.

“When he went up to the holy altar, he made the garment of holiness honourable”, because he was righteous. He stood by the hearth of the altar “as a young cedar in Libanus”, in Lebanon, “and as palm trees compassed they him round about. So were all the sons of Aaron in their glory”: like the moon at the full, like the morning star, at noon.

When you are full of light, you are in your glory. Keep that in mind.

note.label: Gentiles: What Happened to Northern Kingdom?

precepts.why:
“They have moved me to jealousy with that which is not God; they have provoked me to anger with their vanities: and I will move them to jealousy with those which are not a people; I will provoke them to anger with a foolish nation.” Those which are not a people, a foolish nation: the same words as Ecclesiasticus 50, the foolish people that dwell in Shechem. That is talking about the northern kingdom.

So even after all those kings of Assyria came through, remnants of Ephraim remained in the land, and they were still stupid; that is the foolish people of Shechem.

points: “They that sit upon the mountain of Samaria”: the Greeks, because the Greeks took over Samaria. Write that down: those that sit upon Samaria, put a parentheses and put Greeks. “And they that dwell among the Philistines”: Hamites. He despised those two nations; they were always our mortal enemies.
“And that foolish people that dwell in Sichem.” Sichem is a Latinized version of the word; it is Shechem, the capital of Ephraim. That foolish people is the northern kingdom.
In verse 25 he says they’re no nation, not a people. Why? Because they would be broken, based upon Isaiah 7:8.
